title: The Real Presence
hookLine: Catholics teach bread and wine become Christ's body and blood; the Orthodox affirm the change and call it mystery

lines: MANY WALKED NO MORE WITH HIM.
cards: "This is an hard saying; who can hear it?" Many of his own disciples say it in the sixth chapter of John, in a synagogue in Capernaum.
Jesus has just told them that unless they eat his flesh and drink his blood, they have no life in them. Readers still argue over how he meant it.
John says that from that time many of his disciples went back, and walked no more with him. Then Jesus turns to the twelve: "Will ye also go away?"
Peter answers for them, honestly: "Lord, to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life." He doesn't claim to understand. He stays.

teach.b: Fast forward to the night before he died. Jesus takes bread, blesses it, breaks it, and says: "Take, eat; this is my body." Then the cup: "this is my blood."

Paul asks the Corinthians: "The bread which we break, is it not the communion of the body of Christ?" What does "is" mean at that table? Day one hundred fifty-three gave short answers; this takes two days.
Today, two churches that answer: really, truly is. Catholics teach that at the consecration in the Mass, the bread and wine become the body and blood of Christ.
Transubstantiation is the word Catholic councils used to name that change. It borrows an old distinction from philosophy: what a thing really is, its substance, and how it appears to the senses.
The appearances of bread and wine remain: the taste, the color, the crumbs. But what it is has changed.
That's why Catholics kneel or bow before the consecrated host, keep it in a tabernacle, and sit before it in silent adoration.

teach.h: ORTHODOX: A REAL CHANGE, A MYSTERY.
teach.b: Orthodox Christians also confess that the bread and wine truly become Christ's body and blood, but are wary of defining how.
In the Divine Liturgy the change is prayed for: the priest asks the Holy Spirit to come down on the gifts. They call the sacraments mysteries, and they're content to leave this one there.
Two traditions, one table, each holding its way with reverence.
And Peter again: not now I understand, but to whom shall we go? In John's telling, faith can look like staying with words you can't fully explain.

how: Catholics receive the Eucharist at Mass, bow or kneel before the consecrated host, and keep it in a tabernacle for adoration; Orthodox Christians receive the holy gifts in the Divine Liturgy, confessing a real change and calling it a mystery.

o: bread and wine turning into flesh you can see
the moment bread is shared out to the people
a change in what bread and wine are, not how they look

games.q: who says what at the table — tap the pairs.
p: a real change, held as a mystery

s: in Catholic teaching, the bread stops looking and tasting like bread
the appearances of bread and wine remain; what it is, its substance, has changed.
the Orthodox also confess a real change in the bread and wine
they confess it and call it a mystery, without defining how.
in John 6, the twelve leave along with the others
Jesus asks them, "will ye also go away?" and Peter answers for them that they'll stay.

games.q: you're Peter. crowds are walking away over a hard saying, and Jesus asks if you'll go too. what do you say?
games.why: Peter doesn't claim to understand: "to whom shall we go? thou hast the words of eternal life." he stays.

practice: Bring to mind something you can't fully explain and can't quite dismiss: a love, a grief, a moment larger than itself, or, if you receive communion, the bread and the cup.
Don't solve it; if it feels right, bow your head slightly, as people do at the altar. If you pray, offer that bow to God; if you don't, let it simply be respect.

wordCard.voice: Transubstantiation. The Catholic word for bread and wine becoming Christ's body and blood, while their appearances remain.

orig.note: Greek: a mystery — the Orthodox word for a sacrament.

carryVoice: Your line: a holy mystery. Peter didn't understand it all, and still he stayed. See you tomorrow.
